items.body:
### What happened?

#140881 was a total loss of exec readiness probing during the entire graceful termination window, shipped in v1.35.0 and caught by a user, not by CI. Nothing in the e2e suite asserts anything about probes after a pod's `deletionTimestamp` is set.

`test/e2e/common/node/container_probe.go` covers startup, ordering, timeouts, restart counts, and readiness before delete, but every readiness assertion happens while the pod is running normally. `test/e2e/node/pod_termination*.go` and the graceful-shutdown tests cover termination but assert on lifecycle, not readiness. So the probe path and the termination path are each well covered and the intersection is not covered at all.

The unit regression test added in #140882 (`TestProbeWorkersSurviveSyncContextCancellation`) pins the specific context plumbing, but it fakes the pod worker's cancellation. It would not catch a different regression that breaks probing during termination somewhere else in the stack, e.g. in `pod_workers.go` or in the CRI call path.

Filed as a follow-up to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140882#discussion_r3659065740, per @SergeyKanzhelev's request to keep the e2e work out of the backport-able patch.

### What did you expect to happen?

An e2e test that deletes a pod whose readiness probe starts failing on SIGTERM and asserts the pod's `Ready` condition flips to `False` well before the grace period ends.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

N/A, this is a coverage gap. To confirm it: revert #140882 on master and run `test/e2e/common/node` plus the node e2e probe suites. Everything passes.

### Anything else we need to know?

Sketch of the test, matching the manual repro in #140881:

- busybox container that touches `/tmp/ready`, traps `TERM` with `rm -f /tmp/ready; sleep 300`, then idles.
- exec readiness probe `cat /tmp/ready`, `periodSeconds: 1`, `failureThreshold: 1`.
- `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60`.
- Wait for `Ready=True`, delete the pod, then assert `Ready=False` within ~10s, with the pod still in `Terminating`.

Two traps worth writing into the test as comments so the next person does not re-learn them:

1. Assert on the pod's `Ready` condition, not on EndpointSlice membership. The `deletionTimestamp` withdraws the endpoint immediately regardless of readiness, which masks the bug completely.
2. The grace period has to be long enough that the container is still alive when the assertion runs, otherwise the test passes for the wrong reason.

Coverage worth adding beyond the base case, in rough priority order:

1. exec readiness probe during termination (the actual regression).
2. HTTP readiness probe during termination. Not affected by #140881 because the HTTP prober does not take the probe context, but it is the same contract and nothing pins it.
3. Readiness recorded during termination is reflected in the pod status, so a preStop hook that intentionally fails readiness behaves as documented.

Home is probably `test/e2e/common/node/container_probe.go`. It should not be a `ConformanceIt` initially, since it asserts kubelet timing behavior rather than an API guarantee, but it is a reasonable promotion candidate later.

Happy to take this one. PR to follow once #140882 merges, so the test lands against the fixed behavior rather than a known-red baseline.

Related: #140881, #140882, #130487

items.title: kubelet: stopping a probe worker does not cancel an in-flight exec probe

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

items.body:
### What happened?

Stopping a probe worker does not cancel a probe that is already executing. `worker.stop()` does a non-blocking send on `stopCh`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L204-L211

and `run()` only selects on `stopCh` between probes, after `doProbe` returns:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L186-L201

So when `RemovePod` / `CleanupPods` / `StopLivenessAndStartup` stops a worker, an exec probe that is mid-flight keeps running against a container that is being killed. It ends only when its own `TimeoutSeconds` elapses, and `runProbeWithRetries` will retry up to `maxProbeRetries` (3) if the attempt errors, so the worst case is roughly `3 * TimeoutSeconds` after `stop()`. `TimeoutSeconds` is user-controlled, so that can be minutes. The worker also records the result of that last probe after it was told to stop.

Between #130487 (v1.35.0) and #140882 this happened to be papered over: workers inherited the pod worker's sync context, which the pod worker cancels at teardown, so in-flight execs died promptly. That was not a fix, it was the cause of #140881. The same cancellation also killed every readiness probe for the entire grace period, which is the much worse bug. #140882 detaches the worker context with `context.WithoutCancel` and restores the pre-1.35 behavior, which reinstates this gap.

Filed as a follow-up to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140882#discussion_r3659050743.

### What did you expect to happen?

`stop()` cancels the probe that is currently executing, and the worker goroutine exits promptly instead of waiting out `TimeoutSeconds`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Pod with an exec readiness probe whose command blocks (`sleep 300`) and `timeoutSeconds: 60`, plus `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 1`. Delete the pod while a probe is in flight and watch `--v=4` kubelet logs: the `Exec-Probe runProbe` for that worker has no matching completion until the timeout fires, well after the container is gone.

### Anything else we need to know?

Suggested fix: give each worker its own context derived from the (detached) manager context and cancel it from `stop()`, roughly:

1. In `newWorker`, `w.ctx, w.cancel = context.WithCancel(ctx)`.
2. `run()` uses `w.ctx` for `doProbe` and adds `<-w.ctx.Done()` to the select.
3. `stop()` calls `w.cancel()` in addition to signalling `stopCh`, so an in-flight `ExecSync` is cancelled.

That keeps the worker lifecycle owned by the prober manager instead of the pod worker, which is what #140882 is after, while still bounding shutdown.

Worth checking as part of this whether cancelling mid-probe can record a spurious result. `doProbe` throws away errored results today, which is what made #140881 invisible, so a cancelled probe should not flip readiness either way. A test for "stop() during an in-flight probe records no result" would be good to have alongside.

Related: #140881, #140882, #130487

Title
Ensure Credential Pulled Images tests still flaking with "pulled record ... never appeared" after 
#138527/
#138642

Body

Hitting this on kubelet-gce-e2e-swap-ubuntu-serial - pretty sure this is the same flake as 
#136546/
#138527, just came back.

Testgrid: https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-kubelet#kubelet-gce-e2e-swap-ubuntu-serial

A few sub-tests under Ensure Credential Pulled Images ... [FeatureGate:KubeletEnsureSecretPulledImages] are failing, all through the same shared BeforeEach helper (tempRemoveImagePulledRecord in test/e2e_node/util_kubeletconfig.go):

util_kubeletconfig.go:133] Unexpected error: the file with the pulled record for the image ID never appeared:
<context.deadlineExceededError>: context deadline exceeded
Quick rundown of what that helper does: it polls every 1s for up to 5s waiting for kubelet to write an ImagePulledRecord at /var/lib/kubelet/image_manager/pulled/sha256-<hash>, then moves it aside so a later step can check kubelet's behavior when the record's missing. If nothing shows up in 5s, it just fails.

#138527 got closed by 
#138642, but looking at that PR, it only added debug logging to this wait loop - didn't touch the 5s timeout or actually figure out why the record's sometimes missing. So this was never really fixed, just made easier to see happening.

And that's actually how I found something new - the extra logging from 
#138642 caught this in a recent run (2026-07-25, ~12:40 UTC) that wasn't visible back when 
#138527 was filed:

util_kubeletconfig.go:116] failed to stat file ".../pulled/sha256-c0a25c4ccec43320c35febdf68a46e03b3f9323eada881535d78d91aa9962741": ... no such file or directory
util_kubeletconfig.go:128] contents of "/var/lib/kubelet/image_manager/pulled": map[
  .../pulled/sha256-fbeb66043fabeed6f125049e44aef32e0b8f9e657a240b5a2091b292bab530f2:
    {"kind":"ImagePulledRecord", ..., "lastUpdatedTime":"2026-07-25T14:26:20Z", ...}
]
So at the moment it fails, the pulled/ directory isn't actually empty - there's a record in there, just for a different image, written ~23 minutes earlier by (presumably) an earlier sub-test in the same run. The record this specific check is waiting for just never shows up in the 5s window.

That makes me think this isn't pure slowness - more likely kubelet just doesn't write a new ImagePulledRecord at all when the image's already cached from an earlier sub-test in the same run, and the poll is timing out waiting for something that was never coming. Would be good to get sig-node's take on whether that's expected - if so, the fix is probably on the test's assumptions, not the timeout.

Checked the last 10 Testgrid columns for this job (~07-24 to 07-26) - failed 3/10 times, 6/20 over a longer window, so it's a real recurring thing, not a one-off. One specific run if useful: prow job 2080994746846679040 (2026-07-25, ~12:40-14:49 UTC), 2 sub-tests failed with this exact error.

labels.name: sig/node

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The Kubelet configuration validation for CPU Manager (`CPUManagerPolicyOptions`) and Topology Manager (`TopologyManagerPolicyOptions`) should support Kubernetes version emulation through `CompatibilityVersion`.

Currently, policy options are validated against static, compile-time lists (`alphaOptions`, `betaOptions`, and `stableOptions`). Instead, validation should determine whether an option is available based on its lifecycle at the emulated Kubernetes version.

Specifically, configuration validation should:

- Evaluate policy option availability using versioned lifecycle information.
- Compare the option's maturity stage against the current emulation version (`DefaultFeatureGate.EmulationVersion()`).
- Respect the corresponding feature gates for that emulated version (for example, `CPUManagerPolicyAlphaOptions`, `CPUManagerPolicyBetaOptions`, and their Topology Manager equivalents).
- Reject policy options that were not available or enabled in the target emulated release.

This would make CPU Manager and Topology Manager configuration validation consistent with the semantics of `CompatibilityVersion`.

### Why is this needed?

`CompatibilityVersion` allows users to run a newer Kubernetes binary while emulating the behavior of an older Kubernetes release. This is important for upgrades, rollbacks, and version-skew testing.

Today, CPU Manager and Topology Manager policy options are validated against static lists compiled into the binary rather than the emulated version. As a result, options introduced or promoted in later Kubernetes releases can be incorrectly accepted when emulating an older version.

For example, `prefer-align-cpus-by-uncorecache` became stable in Kubernetes v1.34. A Kubelet binary running with `CompatibilityVersion=v1.30` should reject this option, but the current validation accepts it because it only checks the binary's built-in option lists.

This creates a configuration compatibility gap where a configuration accepted under version emulation would not have been accepted by an actual Kubelet of that Kubernetes release, weakening the guarantees provided by `CompatibilityVersion`.

Making policy option validation version-aware ensures that Kubelet configuration behaves consistently with the selected emulation version and preserves the expected upgrade and rollback semantics.

items.title: kubelet: serialized pod status sync causes unnecessary cross-pod serialization

labels.name: sig/scalability
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Scalability.

labels.name: sig/node

labels.name: kind/feature

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The bottleneck in high throughput pod churn (> 5 pods / second / node) seems to be the status update from kubelet.  Other controllers rely on this update, so even if the container has started it is not necessarily visible externally.

There are low-hanging opportunities for efficiency improvement: It does a GET before each update, it runs multiple updates for a pod start (though these already coalesce under load), and it does all operations in series on a single worker goroutine, where a batch of pod status updates blocks the next batch.

Proposed fixes:

- Parallelize status syncs with per-pod ordering preserved . This is what #124596 was addressing (closed by triage bot).
- Eliminate the GET — serve the precondition check from the informer/last-known state (also proposed in #123875).
- Two-tier queue — first-time-Ready and deletion-releasing syncs ahead of lower-importance updates; per-pod coalescing means we are already dropping these updates under moderate load - there's no guarantee that clients will observe them as individual updates.

I have a reproducible benchmark harness (kOps + load generator + per-pod tracing across watch/journal/containerd), full artifacts for every number above, and I'm happy to help revive #124596 or review/test an alternative.

If it's helpful, I can also try to figure out how to run the agent-sandbox stress-test on demand against k/k, I think the test is pretty good at capturing a lot of information in a machine readable format, and then generating a report in a human-readable format!



/sig node
/sig scalability
/kind feature


### Why is this needed?

Under sustained pod churn of ~5–9 creates/s per node, the kubelet starts pods quickly (~200ms to containers running when the image is already pulled) but takes 1–2.5 seconds to report that status to the API server. The delay is in the status manager's serialized sync path, and it caps cluster-wide pod-startup throughput for any consumer that keys off pod status (controllers, autoscalers, users). I instrumented this end-to-end on v1.36.2 and can attribute the full latency chain; I believe this revives #123875, which described the same limitation but was closed by the lifecycle bot without triage, along with both fix attempts (#123877, #124596).

https://storage.googleapis.com/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/kubernetes-sigs_agent-sandbox/1204/presubmit-agent-sandbox-benchmarks-kops-gcp-kindnet/2080749074797039616/artifacts/stress-test/report/index.html

Benchmark: 20–40 node clusters (kOps/GCE, n2-standard-8 workers on pd-ssd, c3-standard-22 control plane, v1.36.2), pod create/delete churn (with a wrapping Agent Sandbox CRD). Per-pod lifecycle traced by joining the API watch stream, kubelet journals, and containerd events.

At ~8 pods/s/node (per-pod p50):

| stage |  latency | 
|  ----- |  ------ | 
|  scheduler binding write → kubelet SyncLoop ADD |  0–1ms             | 
|  ADD → pod sandbox creation dispatched (CRI)            | ~3ms              | 
|  dispatch → containers running (PLEG Started)   |  ~150–240ms        | 
|  PLEG Started → status synced to API server     |  1.16s (p90 1.96s) | 

The last stage scales cleanly with churn: 0.01s at ~1 pods/s/node → 0.22s at ~5/s → 0.82s at ~7/s → 1.16s at ~8/s. Meanwhile kubelet's own pod_start_duration_seconds reports ≤0.5s for 99.9% of pods — the SLI clock stops before the reporting delay begins, so the regression is invisible to the standard dashboards.

What we ruled out:

- API server: PATCH pods/status 6.2ms mean server-side at 373/s; APF wait 0.0ms on all priority levels
- Client rate limiter: fully eliminated as a factor — with [kubeAPIQPS=500](https://storage.googleapis.com/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/kubernetes-sigs_agent-sandbox/1283/presubmit-agent-sandbox-benchmarks-kops-gcp-kindnet/2081011556287516672/artifacts/stress-test/report/index.html), rate-limiting waits are 0.00ms across 68k+ main-client requests at peak churn, and the residual delay is still 944ms p50 / 1,287ms p90 at ~9 pods/s/node.  (Note that there is still client-side rate limiting, but it is on the POST endpoint, which I believe is because we're limiting events QPS to limit load on the apiserver)
- Kubelet work time: first-sync (pod_worker_duration{create}) 212ms and flat across load; volume mounts negligible; PLEG relist steady at 1.00–1.03s / 27ms duration; zero "housekeeping took longer" warnings in journals.
- Container runtime: containerd events show creations running up to 10-wide concurrently, ~86% idle, pause-sandbox spans 95ms p50.

Why pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go:

1. One goroutine: syncPod and syncBatch share a single goroutine by design ("to avoid sync races", Start()); every pod's status update on a node funnels through it sequentially.
2. Two round trips per sync: syncPod does a GET then a PATCH (~15–30ms wall time per sync at load). Same amplification #123875 flagged.
3. No importance ordering: syncBatch iterates m.podStatuses — a Go map, i.e. random order. A pod's first-ever Ready transition (which controllers block on) has equal standing with terminal bookkeeping of deleted pods.
4. The coalescing trap (the subtle finding): the per-pod versioned status means a deep queue coalesces a pod's Pending→Running→Ready into fewer PATCHes. This makes the lane partially self-defending against relief: going 20→40 nodes halved per-node churn but syncs-per-pod rose from ~2.4 to ~3.6 as the queue shallowed and coalescing unwound — scale-out yields sublinear improvement.  https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/kubernetes-sigs_agent-sandbox/1276/presubmit-agent-sandbox-benchmarks-kops-gcp-kindnet/2080880843894558720

items.title: Memory Manager AllocatePod re-applies restored pod allocations after kubelet restart

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

items.body:
### What happened?

With pod-scope Topology Manager and `PodLevelResourceManagers` enabled, the static Memory Manager restores pod-level assignments from its checkpoint when kubelet starts. The existing Pods then go through admission again, and Topology Manager calls `AllocatePod` with `AddOperation`.
﻿
`AllocatePod` does not check whether the Pod already has a restored allocation. It calculates the request again and applies it to a machine state which already includes that Pod's reservation.
﻿
Depending on the remaining capacity, this can:
﻿
- reject an existing Pod during post-restart admission because its own allocation is no longer considered free;
- extend or change the previously selected NUMA affinity;
- reserve the same memory a second time, reducing `Free` and increasing `Reserved` and `NumberOfAssignments` again.
﻿
The Pod and container block entries are overwritten, but the additional machine-state accounting remains and is checkpointed.
﻿
﻿

### What did you expect to happen?

Pod-level Memory Manager allocation should be idempotent across kubelet restart.

When a complete allocation for the Pod has been restored from the checkpoint, post-restart admission should preserve the existing pod allocation, container assignments, NUMA affinity, and machine state. It should not consume capacity again or reject the Pod because of its own reservation.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

A deterministic unit test can extend `TestMemoryManagerRestoreState`:

1. Enable `PodLevelResources` and `PodLevelResourceManagers`.
2. Configure static Memory Manager with pod-scope Topology Manager.
3. Create a Guaranteed Pod with pod-level memory requests and limits and one container.
4. Start Memory Manager and call `AllocatePod` once.
5. Save the pod blocks, container blocks, and machine state.
6. Recreate Memory Manager with the same checkpoint directory to simulate kubelet restart.
7. Start the new manager and verify that the state was restored.

items.body:
The e2e test framework has several patterns that cause flakiness, silent resource leaks, and hard-to-debug failures, especially in disruptive tests that restart API servers or control plane components. PR 137832 addresses these across 13 files (185 additions, 41 deletions), touching SIG api-machinery, apps, cloud-provider, network, node, storage, and testing.

Error suppression hides resource leaks. Across the test suite, cleanup code discards errors from Delete calls. In test/e2e/apimachinery/aggregator.go, the cleanupSampleAPIServer function has 10 such calls (APIService, Deployment, Secret, Service, ServiceAccount, RoleBinding, ClusterRoleBinding, ClusterRole) all silently swallowed. Same pattern in test/e2e/apimachinery/apply.go (4 deployments/pods), test/e2e/apps/rc.go (DeleteCollection), and test/e2e/apps/statefulset.go (ConfigMaps in defer blocks). When these fail, resources leak into subsequent tests with zero trace of what went wrong.

No retry on transient API server errors. GetControlPlaneNodes in test/e2e/framework/util.go calls Nodes().List() and immediately fails on any error. During disruptive tests (daemon restarts, etcd failure injection), the API server is expected to be briefly unreachable. The same issue exists in allNodesReady at test/e2e/framework/node/helper.go and RestartNodes at test/e2e/common/util.go. A transient connection refused or 503 kills the entire test instead of retrying. The fix introduces IsRetryableAPIError which checks for connection refused/reset, server timeout, 429, 503, 500, and unexpected server errors, plus a new WaitForControlPlaneNodes that wraps the listing in a polling loop with retry-on-transient logic.

Healthz returns 200 before daemon is ready. RestartDaemonConfig.waitUp in test/e2e/apps/daemon_restart.go considers the daemon ready when /healthz returns HTTP 200. After a kubelet restart, the health endpoint can report ok while kubelet is still recovering. Logs show errors, pods are not yet scheduled. The fix adds verifyDaemonReadiness which SSHes into the node and checks the last 20 lines of /var/log/kubelet.log for error patterns before declaring readiness.

Goroutines not gracefully stopped. In test/e2e/apps/daemon_restart.go, a cache.NewInformer controller is started with go controller.Run(backgroundCtx.Done()). The cleanup calls cancel() but does not wait for the controller goroutine to finish. The fix replaces this with a dedicated stopCh channel and DeferCleanup that closes the channel then sleeps 100ms to allow graceful shutdown.

PVC deletion races with pod references. DeleteAllStatefulSets in test/e2e/framework/statefulset/rest.go has a TODO comment about not checking whether pods still reference PVCs before deleting them. The current code deletes PVCs immediately, which can fail or leave orphaned PVs when pods are still running. The fix lists pods, checks volume references, and only deletes PVCs that are not in use, with foreground propagation.

Duplicated control plane filtering. GetControlPlaneNodes and WaitForControlPlaneNodes both contain the same node filtering logic (check for control-plane label and NoSchedule taint). The second commit extracts this into a shared filterControlPlaneNodes helper.

All changes are in e2e test code, no user-facing impact.

Related issues:
- 109600: prevent the Expect(err).NotTo(HaveOccurred()) and ExpectNoError(err) anti-pattern in e2e tests (same category of error handling problems)
- 86253: sample-apiserver returns error instead of falling back to second Accept type (directly affects the aggregator.go test modified in this PR)
- 135285: GOAWAY are not handled gracefully in apiserver when aggregating (related network error handling)
- 105536: Orphaned pod found, but error not a directory occurred when trying to remove the volumes dir (related resource cleanup issue)

items.body:
### What happened?

Since v1.35.0, exec readiness probes stop working the moment a pod begins graceful termination. Every probe attempt fails client-side with `rpc error: code = Canceled desc = context canceled`, the prober discards errored results, and the pod's `Ready` condition stays frozen at whatever it was before termination began. A pod whose readiness probe starts failing during its grace period is never marked NotReady.

This is a regression from #130487 (`chore(kubelet): migrate prober to contextual logging`, commit b6f6731ab61, first released in v1.35.0). Probe workers previously ran on `context.Background()`. They now inherit the pod worker's sync context via `probeManager.AddPod(ctx, pod)` in `kubelet.SyncPod`, and `pod_workers.go` cancels that context as soon as teardown begins ("Cancelling current pod sync"). Every subsequent CRI `ExecSync` fails immediately. In a 60s grace period I logged 61 consecutive canceled probes.

Only exec probes are affected. The HTTP, TCP, and gRPC probers don't take the ctx.

### What did you expect to happen?

Readiness probes keep running during graceful termination, and a failing probe flips the pod Ready condition to False within a few probe periods. This worked before 1.35 (see the delete-path output in #124648, filed against ~1.30, where READY drops during Terminating).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Pod with `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60` running busybox with a script that touches `/tmp/ready`, traps TERM to `rm -f /tmp/ready; sleep 300`, and idles. Readiness probe: exec `cat /tmp/ready`, `periodSeconds: 1`, `failureThreshold: 1`.

1. Wait for Ready=True.
2. `kubectl delete pod <pod>` and sample `.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status` once per second.

Observed on kindest/node:v1.35.0: Ready stays True for the entire 59s until the containers die. Kubelet events show `Readiness probe errored and resulted in unknown state: rpc error: code = Canceled desc = context canceled` repeating once per probe period (capped at 25 by event spam filtering).

Note: assert on the pod Ready condition, not the EndpointSlice. The deletionTimestamp withdraws the endpoint immediately regardless of readiness, which masks the bug.

### Anything else we need to know?

Mechanism, confirmed at `--v=4`:

1. `pod_workers.go` cancels the pod sync context at teardown start (`status.cancelFn()`, "Cancelling current pod sync").
2. Probe workers were started with that context (`kl.probeManager.AddPod(ctx, pod)` in `SyncPod`; `go w.run(ctx)` in `prober_manager.go`). Ironically this call site sits right above the #113606 TODO warning about exactly this class of problem.
3. `runProbe` passes the ctx into `newExecInContainer`, so `ExecSync` fails instantly with grpc `Canceled`.
4. `worker.doProbe` treats probe errors as "throw away the result", so `results.Failure` is never recorded and `SetContainerReadiness` never fires.

The three `Exec-Probe runProbe` lines per tick are `runProbeWithRetries` (3 attempts). The pattern repeats once per second for the entire grace period: 61 canceled probes total, zero successful or failed results recorded.

</details>

Verified fix: `go w.run(context.WithoutCancel(ctx))` at the three call sites in `prober_manager.go AddPod`. Worker lifetime is already managed by its own stop channel; `WithoutCancel` keeps the logger. With that two-line change on v1.35.0, the same repro flips Ready to False 1s after the delete. Test matrix (same kind node, kubelet binary swapped):

| kubelet | Ready during 60s graceful delete |
|---|---|
| stock v1.35.0 | True the whole time (bug) |
| v1.35.0 + #139167 | True the whole time (unchanged) |
| v1.35.0 + `WithoutCancel` fix | False at 1s |

Related: this is the dominant cause behind #124648's symptom on current versions, and it makes #139167 a no-op as written (its new branch is gated on phase Failed/Succeeded, which a gracefully deleted pod never hits while containers run; on the eviction path its extra probes hit the same canceled context). The `ready = !workerExists` latching issue described by @smarterclayton on #116965 is real but only reachable once this is fixed. No e2e covers readiness during pod deletion; the merged "readiness probe while in preStop" NodeConformance test only exercises the liveness-kill path, where no teardown occurs, which is how this shipped green. It is a combination of the initial beta criteria we scoped out on https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5836, as well as important considerations identified during code review of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140000.

### KEP Beta Criteria
- [ ] Define and implement relevant metrics and events.
- [ ] Define, implement, and link additional comprehensive integration tests in the KEP.
- [ ] Clarify and design co-existence mechanics for workload-aware scheduling (e.g., group-wide coordinated preemption or evaluating pod group health before preempting).
- [ ] Address scenarios where a preemption victim's grace period exceeds the time window allocated for executing the resize operation (e.g., VPA's fallback time limit).
- [ ] Finalize the approach to prevent "double preemption" across scheduler restarts and long grace periods (e.g., evaluating `nominatedNodeName` vs. checking `spec.nodeName` in `DefaultPreemption`).
- [ ] Evaluate whether to solve the risk of additional unnecessary preemption by aligning `NodeResourcesFit` resource accounting logic with the Kubelet's logic (`max(desired, allocated, actual)`) when evaluating deferred pods.
- [ ] Ensure the Deferred resize scheduling cycle includes resources from `pod.status.nodeAllocatableResourceClaimStatuses` if KEP-5517 Alpha2 (DRA) is implemented.

### Implementation PR Follow-ups & Technical Items (PR #140000)
- [ ] **[Node Resources Fit Delta Calculation (`max(0, ...)` Handling)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140000#discussion_r3608175391):** Re-evaluate the `NodeResourcesFit` resource accounting delta logic when calculating a deferred pod's target resource footprint. 
- [ ] **[Observability & Autoscaler Integration](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140000#discussion_r3613628887):** Surface scheduling preemption failure reasons (via Events, appending details/reasons to status conditions like `Deferred`, or updating `PodResizePending`) so users and possibly autoscaling controllers (like VPA) can determine why space could not be made. Ensure that kubelet handles such changes (including consideration for version skew). 
- [ ] **[Binding Phase Refactoring](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140000#discussion_r3609589583):** Evaluate progressing deferred pods through the binding cycle (implementing `Bind()` and updating `PodResizePending`) instead of using `Permit` phase rejections while waiting for Kubelet actuation. This removes waiting pods from the scheduling queue and allows eliminating unnecessary `ScaleUp` queueing hints in `NodeResourcesFit` [(discussion on ScaleUp QHints)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140000#discussion_r3609619666).
- [ ] **[Framework Extension Point (`IsResponsible`)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140000#discussion_r3609616086):** Evaluate introducing a general scheduler extension point interface (`IsResponsible(pod)`) to clean up runtime plugin execution and avoid individual `IsPodResizeDeferred(pod)` checks across multiple plugins.
- [ ] **[Integration Test Refactoring](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140000#discussion_r3614974843):** Refactor new integration tests (`TestDeferredResizeNodePreemptionPolicy` and `TestDeferredResizeQueueingHandlers`) to be table-driven and consider reusing `CoreResourceEnqueueTestCase`.

items.body:
### Which jobs are failing?

All serial node e2e jobs that run the CPU Manager or Memory Manager suites:

- ci-kubernetes-node-kubelet-containerd-resource-managers
- ci-node-crio-resource-managers
- ci-kubernetes-node-swap-ubuntu-serial
- ci-node-crio-swap-serial
- ci-containerd-node-e2e-serial-ec2
- ci-containerd-node-arm64-e2e-serial-ec2
- presubmits pull-kubernetes-node-kubelet-serial-cpu-manager and pull-kubernetes-node-kubelet-serial-cpu-manager-kubetest2 (for PRs rebased on master)

### Which tests are failing?

The first failure lands in the CPU Manager and Memory Manager suites that disable the PodLevelResources feature gate. After that, every later [Serial] test in the run fails in its BeforeAll or BeforeEach step with:

```
[FAILED] Failed to get successful response from /configz: context deadline exceeded
In [BeforeAll] at: k8s.io/kubernetes/test/e2e_node/kubeletconfig/kubeletconfig.go:186
```

Triage clusters (126 and 51 test names, same root cause, split only by ginkgo phase):

- https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?xjob=azure%7Ckops%7Ccrio%7Cautoscaling%7Ccapz%7Cci-kubernetes-verify%7Ccluster-api%7C-cos-%7Cfedora%7Cwindows%7Clocal-e2e%7Calpha-enabled-default%7Cci-gcp%7Cdocker-docker%7Cdocker-containerd%7Cci-minikube%7Ckvm-docker%7Cci-cloud-provider-gcp%7Cnpd-%7Cagentic-sandbox#fe142f553034eead5bbc
- https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?xjob=azure%7Ckops%7Ccrio%7Cautoscaling%7Ccapz%7Cci-kubernetes-verify%7Ccluster-api%7C-cos-%7Cfedora%7Cwindows%7Clocal-e2e%7Calpha-enabled-default%7Cci-gcp%7Cdocker-docker%7Cdocker-containerd%7Cci-minikube%7Ckvm-docker%7Cci-cloud-provider-gcp%7Cnpd-%7Cagentic-sandbox#2624ca6d5446537c85a5

### Since when has it been failing?

Since 2026-07-22. The last green build ran commit faba7e6a94df (merged 01:11 UTC). The first failing builds ran commit 39c618b5c30c (merged 04:09 UTC).

The clusters also contain builds from 2026-07-15 to 2026-07-17. That was the same failure mode, caused by #137150 and fixed by #140631. See the history section below.

### Reason for failure

The kubelet panics at startup while loading the config file the test wrote:

```
panic: failed to merge global and in-flight KubeletConfiguration while setting defaults,
error: PodLevelResourcesFixDefaulting is enabled, but depends on features that are
disabled: [PodLevelResources]
```

Mechanism:

1. #140514 (merged 2026-07-22 02:55 UTC) added the feature gate `PodLevelResourcesFixDefaulting`, enabled by default at Beta, with a declared dependency on `PodLevelResources` in `pkg/features/kube_features.go`.
2. `configureCPUManagerInKubelet` and `configureMemoryManagerInKubelet` in test/e2e_node set `PodLevelResources: false` in the kubelet config for some test variants, and do not disable the new gate.
3. `SetDefaults_KubeletConfiguration` (`pkg/kubelet/apis/config/v1beta1/defaults.go:72`) merges the config gates into a copy of the global gates with `SetFromMap`. The dependency check fails and the code panics.
4. systemd restarts the kubelet, it panics again on the same config, and /configz returns 503 through the API server proxy until the test times out. Every later Serial test in the run then fails the same way.

Evidence: [prow build](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-kubelet-containerd-resource-managers/2079792906901655552) and the [kubelet.log with the panic](https://storage.googleapis.com/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-kubelet-containerd-resource-managers/2079792906901655552/artifacts/n2d-standard-32-cos-125-19216-532-25-913c732d/kubelet.log).

History: this is the second time this exact pattern broke these jobs. #137150 added `PodLevelResourcesFixKubeletQOSClass` (also enabled by default, also depending on PodLevelResources) and broke the same jobs from 2026-07-15 to 2026-07-17. #140631 fixed the tests by disabling that gate by name, so the fix does not cover the new gate. The presubmit that runs these suites (pull-kubernetes-node-kubelet-serial-cpu-manager) is optional and did not run on #140514.

### Anything else we need to know?

This is not only a CI problem. Any kubelet config file that sets `featureGates: {PodLevelResources: false}` now crashes the kubelet at startup, and disabling a Beta gate is a normal thing for a cluster admin to do.

Two possible fixes:

- Short term, repeat #140631 for the new gate: also set `PodLevelResourcesFixDefaulting: false` next to the existing lines in `test/e2e_node/cpu_manager_test.go` and `test/e2e_node/memory_manager_test.go` when the test disables PodLevelResources.
- Longer term, stop the kubelet from panicking here. Either the dependency check should treat a gate that is only enabled by default as off when its dependency is off, or config loading should return an error instead of panicking. Without that, every future gate that depends on PodLevelResources and ships enabled by default will break these jobs again.

items.title: kubelet copies IPv6 link-local scoped nameservers from the node resolv.conf into pods where they cannot work

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

items.body:
### What happened?

With `dnsPolicy: Default`, kubelet copies the node resolv.conf nameservers into the pod verbatim. When the node file contains an IPv6 link-local nameserver with a scope zone, for example `nameserver fe80::29c:2ff:fea9:fdd0%3`, that exact line is written into the pod `/etc/resolv.conf`.

The scope zone is a node interface index. It does not exist in the pod network namespace, so the resolver cannot use the address (socket setup fails with `EINVAL`). This also affects CoreDNS, which runs with `dnsPolicy: Default`, inherits the same file, and forwards to it via `forward . /etc/resolv.conf`. Because the forward plugin distributes across all listed nameservers with the default random policy, a fraction of upstream lookups select the unusable server and fail intermittently with resolution timeouts.

Root cause is in `parseResolvConf` (`pkg/kubelet/network/dns/dns.go`). The nameserver value is appended verbatim with no IP parse, address family, scope, or reachability check. The only later processing is truncation to `MaxDNSNameservers` and dedup:

```go
if fields[0] == "nameserver" {
    if len(fields) >= 2 {
        nameservers = append(nameservers, fields[1])
    }
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

kubelet should not propagate a nameserver that cannot function in the pod network namespace. When the pod does not share the host netns, kubelet should drop IPv6 link-local (`fe80::/10`) nameservers that carry a scope zone. This matches the fix Podman shipped in containers/common#2233 for the same case.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Node running systemd-resolved, with kubelet `--resolv-conf=/run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf` (the kubeadm default when systemd-resolved is detected).
2. Router advertises IPv6 RDNSS via RA, so systemd-resolved writes a scoped link-local nameserver into that file:
   ```
   nameserver 172.16.3.254
   nameserver fe80::29c:2ff:fea9:fdd0%3
   nameserver 2600:1700:76f0:14bf:29c:2ff:fea9:fdd0
   ```
3. Start any pod with `dnsPolicy: Default`. Its `/etc/resolv.conf` contains the `fe80::...%3` line unchanged.
4. From that pod, query the scoped server directly and observe it is unusable in the pod netns:
   ```
   dig @fe80::29c:2ff:fea9:fdd0 example.com
   # UDP setup with fe80::29c:2ff:fea9:fdd0#53 failed: invalid file
   ```
5. Under normal load, external name resolution fails intermittently as the resolver rotates onto the unusable server.

### Anything else we need to know?

- Precedent that this is a resolv.conf hygiene bug, not expected behavior: containers/common#2233 filters link-local nameservers when building a container resolv.conf, with the reasoning that a container has a different interface index so a scoped address can never work. glibc has long declined to support scoped nameservers (Debian bug 455671).
- Related but distinct: #58180 (pods cannot reach IPv6-only upstreams) and the maintainer note in #54773 that inheriting the host DNS config for pods was likely a mistake.
- The same argument applies to any nameserver kubelet cannot verify is usable from the pod netns, but the concrete and low-risk case is the scoped link-local address.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.31.14
Server Version: v1.35.6
```

</details>

### Cloud provider

<details>

None. Bare metal, kubeadm-managed cluster.

</details>

### OS version

<details>

```console
$ cat /etc/os-release
# Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (workers), Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS (control plane)
$ uname -a
Linux vmubtkube-a23 7.0.0-28-generic #28~24.04.1-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Wed Jul  1 15:50:57 UTC 2 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux
```

</details>

### Install tools

<details>

kubeadm

</details>

### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

<details>

cri-o 1.35.4

</details>

### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

<details>

Calico v3.32.1 (Tigera operator install, calico-system namespace), IPv4. Pods have no IPv6 egress route, which is why the scoped link-local and the global IPv6 nameserver are both unusable from the pod netns.

</details>

items.title: DRA device health timeout does not trigger a PodStatus update at the expiration deadline

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: wg/device-management
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to WG Device Management.

items.body:
### What happened?

DRA device health expiration is evaluated lazily. `getHealthInfo` compares `LastUpdated` with the device timeout only when health information is read,`updateHealthInfo` also checks for expired devices that are missing from a complete plugin response, but it runs only when another `NodeWatchResourcesResponse` is received,There is no timer, deadline queue, or periodic worker that transitions a device to `Unknown` when its health-check timeout expires.
﻿
For example:
﻿
1. A plugin reports an allocated device as `Healthy` with a short `health_check_timeout_seconds` value.
2. The stream remains connected, but the plugin stops sending health responses.
3. The timeout expires.
4. No `changedDevices` result is produced because `updateHealthInfo` is not called.
5. No resource update notification is sent for Pods using the device.
﻿
The next call to `getHealthInfo` will calculate `Unknown`, but that read is normally part of rebuilding Pod status. The health timeout itself does not enqueue the affected Pod, so `AllocatedResourcesStatus` can continue showing the previous health value until another pod sync or unrelated update occurs.
﻿
The normal notification path exists only while processing a stream response,
﻿
The default kubelet sync frequency is one minute and is configurable, so the user-visible delay is unrelated to the device-specific health timeout and can be longer:
﻿
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2192afa9f369883debb4bd43a1f9177aeab80a8e/pkg/kubelet/apis/config/v1beta1/defaults.go#L78-L80

### What did you expect to happen?

When a reported device reaches its health-check deadline without a fresh report, kubelet should transition that device to `Unknown` and enqueue every affected Pod for a status update at, or shortly after, the deadline.

The health protocol states that devices not present in the complete list become `Unknown` after a timeout:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2192afa9f369883debb4bd43a1f9177aeab80a8e/staging/src/k8s.io/kubelet/pkg/apis/dra-health/v1alpha1/api.proto#L71-L74

KEP-4680's test plan also calls out both behaviors:

- marking devices as `Unknown` after a timeout period;
- properly sending update notifications for affected Pods.

https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/4680-add-resource-health-to-pod-status

A deterministic test can use a fake DRA health stream and an allocated device referenced by a Pod:

1. Start `HandleWatchResourcesStream` with a fake stream.
2. Send a `Healthy` response for the allocated device with a short timeout.
3. Consume the initial Pod update notification.
4. Keep the stream open and send no further responses.
5. Advance a fake clock beyond the device deadline, or wait for the short timeout in an integration-style test.
6. Assert that the DRA manager sends another update for the affected Pod.
7. Rebuild the Pod status and assert that the device is `Unknown` with an empty stale-health message.

With the current implementation, step 6 times out because there is no deadline-driven execution path.

items.body:
### What happened?

During a seamless DRA plugin upgrade, kubelet may have multiple registered plugin endpoints for the same driver. The DRA plugin manager intentionally supports this:
﻿
Regular DRA RPCs select a preferred plugin, favoring the most recently registered connected endpoint,However, health monitoring starts an independent `NodeWatchResources` stream for every registered endpoint,All of those streams call the handler with only the driver name. The endpoint identity or registration generation is not passed to the DRA manager,Health information is also stored per driver, not per plugin endpoint
﻿
This allows responses from old and new endpoints to reconcile the same driver cache concurrently. Because each `NodeWatchResourcesResponse` is a complete list for the driver, a response from the old endpoint can overwrite health information reported by the new endpoint.
﻿
There is a second race during endpoint removal. Deregistration cancels that endpoint's health stream,When any health stream exits, its handler unconditionally clears all health information for the driver,
﻿
Therefore, an old endpoint being deregistered can clear health information that was already reported by the new endpoint.
﻿
The cache transition caused by `clearDriver` also does not notify affected Pods. Pod update notifications are sent only from the normal response-processing path when `updateHealthInfo` returns changed devices,This can leave `AllocatedResourcesStatus` with stale `Healthy` or `Unhealthy` values until another pod sync occurs, even though the internal lookup now returns `Unknown`.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should have one authoritative health stream per driver. During a plugin upgrade, health updates should come only from the most recently registered applicable endpoint, as specified by KEP-4680:
﻿
> For seamless plugin upgrades, where multiple instances of a plugin might run concurrently, the Kubelet will always watch the most recently registered plugin for health updates.
﻿
https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/4680-add-resource-health-to-pod-status
﻿
When ownership moves to a new endpoint:
﻿
- the old stream should be canceled or ignored;
- responses from an older registration generation must not overwrite current state;
- termination of an old stream must not clear state owned by the new stream;
- if the authoritative stream is lost and device health becomes `Unknown`, affected Pods should receive a resource update notification.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

A deterministic unit test can use two fake endpoints registered under the same driver name:
﻿
1. Register endpoint A and let its health stream report device `pool/device` as `Healthy`.
2. Register endpoint B for the same driver and let its stream report the same device as `Unhealthy`.
3. Send another `Healthy` response from endpoint A.
4. Observe that the shared driver cache can be changed by the non-authoritative endpoint A.
5. Deregister endpoint A, which cancels its stream.
6. Observe that A's deferred `clearDriver(driverName)` removes the state reported by endpoint B.
7. Observe that this cache clear does not place an update for the affected Pod on the DRA manager update channel.
﻿
The test should assert that only endpoint B can update the cache after B becomes authoritative, that A's termination cannot clear B's state, and that losing the authoritative stream notifies affected Pods when their reported health changes to `Unknown`.

items.body:
### What happened?

With the static Memory Manager and pod-level Topology Manager scope, `getPodRequestedResources` drops a memory resource type when that resource is requested by a regular init container but by no app container.
﻿
A minimal example is:
﻿
- a regular init container requests `memory: 1Gi` and `hugepages-1Gi: 2Gi`;
- the app container requests `memory: 1Gi`, but does not request `hugepages-1Gi`.
﻿
The calculated pod request is:
﻿
```text
map[memory:1073741824]
```
﻿
The expected result is:
﻿
```text
map[hugepages-1Gi:2147483648 memory:1073741824]
```
﻿
The init container still receives an individual hugepage memory block because its resources are processed separately, but the pod allocation and global NUMA capacity do not account for that block. This can produce incorrect topology hints and leave the Memory Manager machine state with more available hugepage capacity than actually assigned.

### What did you expect to happen?

getPodRequestedResources` should calculate each managed resource independently across the union of resource names requested by:
﻿
- app containers;
- restartable init containers;
- regular init containers.
﻿
For every resource name, the existing init-container and long-running-container maximum semantics should then be applied. A resource must not be omitted merely because no app container requests that resource type.
﻿
In the example above, both `memory` and `hugepages-1Gi` must be included in topology hint generation, pod memory blocks, and NUMA machine-state accounting.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Add the following case to `Test_getPodRequestedResources` in `pkg/kubelet/cm/memorymanager/policy_static_test.go`:

`{
	description: "resource requested only by a regular init container",
	pod: getPodWithInitContainers(
		"",
		[]v1.Container{
			{
				Name: "app-container",
				Resources: v1.ResourceRequirements{
					Requests: v1.ResourceList{
						v1.ResourceMemory: resource.MustParse("1Gi"),
					},
				},
			},
		},
		[]v1.Container{
			{
				Name: "init-container",
				Resources: v1.ResourceRequirements{
					Requests: v1.ResourceList{
						v1.ResourceMemory: resource.MustParse("1Gi"),
						hugepages1Gi:      resource.MustParse("2Gi"),
					},
				},
			},
		},
	),
	expected: map[v1.ResourceName]uint64{
		v1.ResourceMemory: 1 * gb,
		hugepages1Gi:      2 * gb,
	},
},
`

go test ./pkg/kubelet/cm/memorymanager -run Test_getPodRequestedResources -count=1

items.body:
### What happened?

/kind bug
/sig scheduling
/sig node
/wg device-management

The structured allocator derives per-pool state about already-allocated devices from the current ResourceSlice contents. Slices are mutable, so a driver can republish a pool without a previously-allocated device, or with different `ConsumesCounters` for it - and when that happens, the allocated device's contribution silently disappears from the allocator's accounting. This affects two features with different severity:

**1. PartitionableDevices: counter availability can be over-committed.**

`checkAvailableCounters` (`staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go`, mirrored in the incubating and stable allocators) computes per-pool availability by starting from the counter set totals and subtracting the consumption of allocated devices **found in the current slices**. An allocated device that is no longer published (or whose `ConsumesCounters` changed) no longer subtracts anything, so the pool appears to have more counters free than it physically does, and new allocations can over-commit the shared counters of a device that is still in use. 

**2. DRADeviceCompatibilityGroups (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139795): the enforcement baseline loses allocated peers.**

`compatibilityGroupsBaselineForPool` deliberately copies the counters pattern (its comment: "exactly like checkAvailableCounters does for counters"): group *values* come from the allocation-time snapshot in the claim status, but counter-set *membership* still comes from the current slice. If the allocated device is not in the republished slice, its intersection contribution drops out of the feature-on baseline and a later incompatible device can be admitted onto the counter set. Notably, the feature-off version-skew skip (`groupedCounterSetsFromState`) is built purely from snapshots and keeps protecting the same counter set - the enforcement path is less conservative than the skip path.

### What did you expect to happen?

Accounting and enforcement for already-allocated devices should depend only on allocation-time state, never on the current slice contents, which the compatibility-groups KEP already designates as unsafe for enforcement (that is the snapshot's entire purpose).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```
diff --git a/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/allocatortesting/allocator_testing.go b/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/allocatortesting/allocator_testing.go
index 0812be3023c..505c6fe5df9 100644
--- a/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/allocatortesting/allocator_testing.go
+++ b/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/allocatortesting/allocator_testing.go
@@ -3539,6 +3539,46 @@ func TestAllocator(t *testing.T,
 				deviceAllocationResult(req1, driverA, pool1, device3, false),
 			)},
 		},
+		// device1 is allocated, but the driver has republished the pool
+		// without it. How much it consumed is recorded nowhere: the slice no
+		// longer declares the device, and the allocated state carries only
+		// its ID - there is no allocation-time record of counter
+		// consumption. The premise of this scenario is that device1 consumed
+		// the entire 8Gi counter when it was allocated, so granting device2
+		// (which needs all 8Gi) over-commits the physical counter. The
+		// allocator must not hand out counters it cannot account for; the
+		// allocated DeviceID names this pool, so the unaccounted device is
+		// detectable even without a consumption record.

+			features: Features{

+			claimsToAllocate: objects(claimWithRequest(claim0, req0, classA)),
+			allocatedDevices: []DeviceID{
```

items.title: DRA: disabling allowMultipleAllocations in a ResourceSlice update keeps a capacity requestPolicy that create validation rejects

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

labels.name: wg/device-management
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to WG Device Management.

items.body:
/kind bug
/sig node
/wg device-management

**What happened?**

`ValidateResourceSliceUpdate` re-validates a device's `capacity` only when the capacity itself has changed:

```go
// pkg/apis/resource/validation/validation.go
if oldDevice == nil || !apiequality.Semantic.DeepEqual(oldDevice.Capacity, device.Capacity) {
    if allowMultipleAllocations {
        // validateMultiAllocatableDeviceCapacity: validates requestPolicy
    } else {
        // validateSingleAllocatableDeviceCapacity: forbids requestPolicy
    }
}
```

However, which capacity validator applies depends on the device's effective `allowMultipleAllocations` value.

An update can therefore change `allowMultipleAllocations` from `true` to `false` (or unset it) while leaving `capacity` unchanged. Because the capacity remains semantically equal according to `apiequality.Semantic.DeepEqual`, capacity validation is skipped.

If the unchanged capacity contains a `requestPolicy`, the resulting object is accepted with this invalid combination:

```yaml
allowMultipleAllocations: false
capacity:
  cap:
    value: 1Gi
    requestPolicy:
      default: 1Mi
      validRange:
        min: 1Mi
```

The same object would be rejected during create validation by `validateSingleAllocatableDeviceCapacity` with:

```text
requestPolicy: Forbidden: allowMultipleAllocations must be true
```

Although the capacity value is unchanged, this is not a no-op update of an untouched stored value: changing `allowMultipleAllocations` changes the validation regime and semantics that apply to the capacity.

**What did you expect to happen?**

An update that changes the effective `allowMultipleAllocations` value from `true` to `false` while retaining a capacity `requestPolicy` should be rejected with:

```text
requestPolicy: Forbidden: allowMultipleAllocations must be true
```

The same should apply when the field changes from `true` to unset, because unset and `false` have the same effective meaning.

**How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?**

Add this case to `TestValidateResourceSliceUpdate` in `pkg/apis/resource/validation/validation_resourceslice_test.go`:

```go
"disable-allow-multiple-keeps-request-policy": {
    consumableCapacityFeatureGate: true,
    oldResourceSlice:              testResourceSliceWithConsumableCapacity(name, name, name, 1),
    update: func(slice *resourceapi.ResourceSlice) *resourceapi.ResourceSlice {
        slice.Spec.Devices[0].AllowMultipleAllocations = ptr.To(false)
        return slice
    },
    wantFailures: field.ErrorList{
        field.Forbidden(
            field.NewPath("spec", "devices").
                Index(0).
                Child("capacity").
                Key("a").
                Child("requestPolicy"),
            "allowMultipleAllocations must be true",
        ),
    },
},
```

Run:

```console
go test ./pkg/apis/resource/validation \
  -run 'TestValidateResourceSliceUpdate/disable-allow-multiple-keeps-request-policy' \
  -count=1
```

The test fails on master because `ValidateResourceSliceUpdate` returns no error.

An equivalent test which sets `AllowMultipleAllocations = nil` instead of `ptr.To(false)` also reproduces the bug.

**Anything else we need to know?**

A candidate fix is to re-run capacity validation when either the capacity changes or the device's effective `allowMultipleAllocations` value changes:

```go
// Capacity validation selects the multi- vs single-allocatable validator by the effective
// allowMultipleAllocations, so it must re-run when that value changes even if the capacity is unchanged.
oldAllowMultipleAllocations := oldDevice != nil &&
    oldDevice.AllowMultipleAllocations != nil &&
    *oldDevice.AllowMultipleAllocations

if oldDevice == nil ||
    allowMultipleAllocations != oldAllowMultipleAllocations ||
    !apiequality.Semantic.DeepEqual(oldDevice.Capacity, device.Capacity) {
    if allowMultipleAllocations {
        allErrs = append(allErrs,
            validateMap(
                device.Capacity,
                -1,
                attributeAndCapacityMaxKeyLength,
                validateQualifiedName,
                validateMultiAllocatableDeviceCapacity,
                fldPath.Child("capacity"),
            )...,
        )
    } else {
        allErrs = append(allErrs,
            validateMap(
                device.Capacity,
                -1,
                attributeAndCapacityMaxKeyLength,
                validateQualifiedName,
                validateSingleAllocatableDeviceCapacity,
                fldPath.Child("capacity"),
            )...,
        )
    }
}
```

The comparison uses the effective boolean value, so `nil` and `false` remain equivalent and do not trigger unnecessary revalidation when changing between those two representations.

This has the same reachable `allowMultipleAllocations: true -> false` transition as #140797, but it is a separate validation-layer bug: #140797 concerns allocator exclusivity, while this issue concerns accepting a ResourceSlice state that create validation forbids.

Happy to send a fix.

**Kubernetes version**

master, with `DRAConsumableCapacity` enabled.

items.title: DRA: dedicated allocation can overlap a live persisted shared allocation after allowMultipleAllocations is disabled

labels.name: kind/bug

items.body:
/kind bug
/sig node
/wg device-management

**What happened?**

In the structured DRA allocator, `deviceInUse(deviceID)` gates exclusive (dedicated) allocation in `allocateDevice`, but it only checks `AllocatedDevices` and the in-flight `allocatingDeviceForAnyClaim`. It does not check `AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs`. So `deviceInUse` never blocks a device that carries a live persisted share, and in states where no other capacity check happens to stop the request, that device can be handed out as a dedicated allocation to another claim. The result is a device that is dedicated to one claim and shared by another at the same time.

The reachable trigger is an `allowMultipleAllocations` true->false change in a ResourceSlice update while a share is still live. `ValidateResourceSliceUpdate` only makes `spec.pool.name`, `spec.driver`, and `spec.nodeName` immutable, so this flip passes API validation. After it, the device is treated as dedicated, and `deviceInUse` still does not see the persisted share.

This is the same class as #140437, which taught `deviceCapacityInUse` to recognize persisted shares. `IsDeviceAllocated` recognizes them too; `deviceInUse` is the remaining allocation gate that does not.

**What did you expect to happen?**

A device with a live persisted share should not be allocated dedicated on top of that share.

**How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?**

Add this case to `allocatortesting` and run `TestAllocator` for the experimental (or incubating) allocator. It fails on master: `device-1` is allocated dedicated (`ShareID: nil`) even though it has a live persisted share.

```go
"dedicated-request-not-blocked-by-persisted-share": {
	// device1 carries a persisted shared allocation (share ID), but the slice
	// now advertises it as an ordinary, non-allow-multiple device: an
	// AllowMultipleAllocations true->false flip while the share is still live.
	// deviceInUse must still see the persisted share and refuse to hand device1
	// out as a dedicated allocation on top of the live share.
	features: Features{ConsumableCapacity: true},
	allocatedSharedDeviceIDs: sets.New(
		internal.MakeSharedDeviceID(MakeDeviceID(driverA, pool1, device1), &fixedShareID),
	),
	claimsToAllocate: objects(claimWithRequests(claim0, nil, request(req0, classA, 1))),
	classes:          objects(class(classA, driverA)),
	slices: unwrapResourceSlices(
		sliceWithDevices(slice1, node1, resourcePool(pool1, 1), driverA,
			device(device1, nil, nil),
		),
	),
	node:          node(node1, region1),
	expectResults: []any{},
},
```

**Anything else we need to know?**

Scope, precisely: `deviceInUse` does not block any persisted shared allocation. Where no other capacity check coincidentally rejects the request (for example the minimal reproducer above, whose device has no capacity and no capacity request), this directly produces a dedicated-over-shared allocation. A device with non-empty consumed capacity may instead be stopped by `CmpRequestOverCapacity`, so this is an unreliable exclusivity check rather than a guarantee that every capacity-bearing share is double-allocated.

On a fix: making `deviceInUse` itself recognize shares (e.g. calling `IsDeviceAllocated`) is not correct on its own. It would reject a legitimate further share of an allow-multiple device; I confirmed it makes the `partitionable-consumable-capacity-shared-device-counter-not-recharged` case (from #140437) fail. The fix also has to keep AdminAccess, which is meant to reach in-use devices, so the new check must stay under the existing `!request.adminAccess()` guard. One shape that keeps AdminAccess and passes both modes is to reject a dedicated candidate when its capacity is in use, next to the existing check:

```go
if !request.adminAccess() && !allowMultipleAllocations && alloc.deviceCapacityInUse(device.id) {
	return false, nil, nil
}
```

`deviceCapacityInUse` already recognizes persisted shares since #140437. The experimental and incubating allocators share this code; the stable allocator does not support these features. Happy to send a fix.

**Kubernetes version**

master (DRA structured allocator, experimental + incubating). Required for the minimal reproducer: `DRAConsumableCapacity`. `DRAPartitionableDevices` is not required; it is only relevant to the related #140437 regression case.

/cc @mortent @pohly

labels.name: kind/bug

items.body:
### What happened?

CRI runtimes provide labels like `id`, `name`, and `image`, but not the Kubernetes-level `namespace`, `pod`, and `container` labels. The cadvisor path adds these via `containerPrometheusLabelsFunc` in `pkg/kubelet/server/server.go`, but the CRI path has no equivalent.

This means any monitoring setup that queries by `namespace`, `pod`, or `container` on cadvisor metrics (which is most of them) breaks when the feature gate is turned on.

### What did you expect to happen?

`/metrics/cadvisor` should produce the same label set regardless of whether the cadvisor or CRI stats path is active.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Enable `PodAndContainerStatsFromCRI` feature gate on the kubelet
2. Run a workload
3. Scrape `/metrics/cadvisor`
4. Observe that metrics like `container_cpu_usage_seconds_total` are missing `namespace`, `pod`, and `container` labels

### Anything else we need to know?

Two approaches:

**Option 1: Kubelet resolves labels at scrape time**

Call `ListPodSandbox` and `ListContainers` in the metrics collector to build sandbox/container ID → metadata maps, then append `namespace`, `pod`, `container` to each metric. This follows the same pattern `criStatsProvider.getPodAndContainerMaps` uses for `/stats/summary`. The two RPCs are local gRPC calls and the scrape interval is typically 30s, so the cost is low.

**Option 2: Extend the CRI API**

`ListPodSandboxMetrics` currently returns metrics keyed by sandbox/container ID, but without any pod or container metadata. The runtime already has this metadata, it receives `PodSandboxMetadata` (name, namespace, uid) during `RunPodSandbox` and `ContainerMetadata` (name) during `CreateContainer`, and stores both for the lifetime of the sandbox/container.

Adding these existing metadata fields to `PodSandboxMetrics` and `ContainerMetrics` would let the kubelet read `namespace`, `pod`, and `container` directly from the metrics response without any additional RPCs or cache lookups.

A lighter variant: only add the pod UID to `PodSandboxMetrics`. The kubelet can then look up name and namespace from its internal pod cache (keyed by UID), and resolve container names by matching container IDs against the cached pod status.

/kind bug

items.title: kubelet's CSI PluginWatcher goroutine never fires — permanently idle `select` from process start, despite a valid pre-existing registration socket

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/node
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Node.

labels.name: needs-triage

items.body:
### What happened?

**Disclosure: this report was prepared with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic).** The
diagnostic work (goroutine dump capture/analysis, ruling out environmental causes, reading
the relevant kubelet source) was done by an AI coding assistant under the direct
supervision of the cluster operator (a human), who reviewed and approved each diagnostic
step before it was run against the live cluster. This was originally filed against
k3s-io/k3s (see https://github.com/k3s-io/k3s/issues/14418) — the maintainers there
correctly pointed out that pkg/kubelet/pluginmanager/pluginwatcher is unmodified
upstream code, not something k3s patches, and asked that it be reported here instead with
this disclosure included.

kubelet never completes the CSI plugin registration handshake for any CSI driver, on any
node in the cluster. `kubectl get csinode <node>` shows `DRIVERS: 0` indefinitely,
regardless of how many times the CSI driver pod, its registration socket, kubelet, or the
whole node is restarted/rebooted.

The CSI driver's own node-driver-registrar sidecar behaves exactly as expected on its side:
I0720 13:51:22.943288       1 node_register.go:56] "Starting Registration Server" socketPath="/registration/driver.longhorn.io-reg.sock"
I0720 13:51:22.943661       1 node_register.go:66] "Registration Server started" socketPath="/registration/driver.longhorn.io-reg.sock"


No ReceiveNotifyRegistrationStatus call is ever logged afterward — kubelet's plugin-watcher never dials back.

Root cause, pinpointed via kubelet's own pprof goroutine dump (captured safely via
kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=2" — read-only,
no config changes, no restarts):

goroutine 1417 [select, 42 minutes]:
k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/pluginmanager/pluginwatcher.(*Watcher).Start.func1(0x3c5e9cd02ba0)
	pkg/kubelet/pluginmanager/pluginwatcher/plugin_watcher.go:74 +0x110
created by k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/pluginmanager/pluginwatcher.(*Watcher).Start in goroutine 1428
	pkg/kubelet/pluginmanager/pluginwatcher/plugin_watcher.go:72 +0x3de

This is the PluginWatcher's event-processing loop (Watcher.Start's internal goroutine,
which reads from the underlying fsnotify.Watcher's event/error channels). It sits in
this select from the moment the goroutine is created, having processed zero events for
its entire lifetime — confirmed by capturing this goroutine dump twice, ~1 minute apart,
with the idle duration advancing by exactly the elapsed wall-clock time (42 minutes →
43 minutes), i.e. it never once returns from the select to handle anything.

To directly rule out any container/mount-namespace-propagation explanation, we created a
real Unix domain socket directly on the node's host filesystem (via
python3 -c "import socket; s=socket.socket(socket.AF_UNIX, socket.SOCK_STREAM);
s.bind('<kubelet-root-dir>/plugins_registry/test-manual.sock')", i.e. not through any
container) in the exact directory traversePluginDir() watches. Captured the same
goroutine immediately before and ~1 minute after creating this file: [select, 42
minutes] → [select, 43 minutes] — no reaction whatsoever, and zero related log lines in
kubelet's own log for that window.

A separate fsnotify-backed watcher in the same kubelet process,
k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/util/filesystem.(*fsnotifyWatcher) (used for watching certificate
files), is present, distinct, and functions normally — this rules out a systemic
inotify/fsnotify failure on the host; the break is isolated specifically to the CSI

### What did you expect to happen?

kubectl get csinode <node> should show the registered CSI driver, and
node-driver-registrar's log should show a ReceiveNotifyRegistrationStatus call:
&RegistrationStatus{PluginRegistered:true...} line shortly after "Registration Server
started" — matching the behavior this exact cluster had reliably, for months, prior to
this incident.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Not yet reduced to a minimal repro outside this cluster — reproducibility was instead
established by exhaustively ruling out every plausible cause specific to this
environment (see "Anything else" below). We were unable to identify a specific trigger;
this appears to be a bug that was already present for some unknown period before
being noticed, invisible until a node genuinely needed a fresh CSI registration
handshake.

### Anything else we need to know?

Environmental causes ruled out, each with direct evidence:
- Restarting the CSI driver pod (fresh registrar process, fresh socket) — no change.
- Restarting kubelet (systemctl restart k3s-agent) repeatedly, on multiple nodes — no change.
- Full node reboot (multiple nodes, multiple times) — no change.
- Fully deleting and recreating the CSI driver's DaemonSet — no change.
- Different CSI sidecar (node-driver-registrar) versions, two tested — identical failure on both.
- Kernel version: the nodes had picked up a kernel bump shortly before the issue was
  first noticed, initially suspected as an inotify regression. Tested directly via
  grub-reboot back into the previously-good kernel (confirmed via uname -r
  post-reboot) — identical failure. Kernel is not the cause.
- AppArmor: no denials logged; more importantly, kubelet itself isn't confined by any
  AppArmor profile at all on this host.
- A shadowing mount over the plugin registration directory — checked via findmnt, not present.
- inotify limits (fs.inotify.max_user_watches, max_user_instances) — nowhere near exhausted.
- A stale/duplicate leftover from a previously-removed CSI driver confusing the
  directory traversal — checked directory contents directly, nothing unusual present.
- Clean-slate test: stopped kubelet entirely, deleted all contents of both the plugin
  registration directory and the plugin socket directory, restarted kubelet from an
  empty state, let the CSI driver pod recreate its socket fresh — identical failure.

Timeline: the kubelet/node in question had been running without a fresh CSI
registration need for an extended period (weeks) before this was noticed — we believe
this is a latent bug that doesn't manifest until a plugin registration is actually
attempted fresh (e.g. after a kubelet or node restart that happens to coincide with a CSI
driver pod restart), rather than something that broke at a specific moment.

fsnotify version (vendored dependency used by pluginwatcher): github.com/fsnotify/fsnotify
v1.9.0 — checked v1.9.0's release notes, nothing in the changelog obviously matches this
symptom (fixes there were about a duplicate-watch panic and a race during path deletion,
not "Add() silently registers no watch on an ordinary, pre-existing directory").

### Kubernetes version

v1.36.2 (k3s build: v1.36.2+k3s1, go1.26.4)


### Cloud provider

Self-hosted, bare VMs (Proxmox). 3-node cluster (1 control-plane + 2 workers).


### OS version

Ubuntu 24.04

items.body:
### What happened?

Historically, memory requests in Kubernetes were not mapped to Linux cgroup constructs (unlike CPU requests, which map to cpu.shares / cpu.weight). Because cgroups did not enforce or track memory requests, kubelet status reporting logic (convertToAPIPodLevelResourcesStatus and convertContainerStatusResources) bypassed cgroups for memory requests and instead relied on spec values or previous status values.

With the introduction of MemoryQoS (MemoryQoS feature gate using TieredReservationMemoryReservationPolicy), memory.min is configured on cgroup v2 for Guaranteed pods based on memory requests and Since memory.min (Guaranteed) and memory.low (Burstable) now reflect memory requests in cgroups when MemoryQoS is enabledmemory.low is configured on cgroup v2 for Burstable pods based on memory requests.

PodStatus and ContainerStatus memory requests are never read back from cgroup state; they are always populated by preserving old status values or aggregating from container/pod specs 

### What did you expect to happen?

Since memory.min (Guaranteed) and memory.low (Burstable) now reflect memory requests in cgroups when MemoryQoS is enabled, Pod status should reflect the values:
- GetPodCgroupConfig / cgroup managers be updated to read memory.min / memory.low as actual cgroup memory request values when MemoryQoS is active and memory.min and memory.low are set

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3d3f9b2f4665b059b50536f114bc7fb1dc831586/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L2472

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3d3f9b2f4665b059b50536f114bc7fb1dc831586/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L2254

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Enable Feature Gates: Enable MemoryQoS=true (with memoryReservationPolicy: TieredReservation) and PodLevelResources=true.
2. Deploy a Guaranteed Pod: Create a pod with requests.memory: 1Gi and limits.memory: 1Gi. Kubelet sets memory.min = 1073741824 on the cgroup v2 path.
3. kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.resources}'

items.body:
### What happened?

Pods that are terminated via node drain / eviction (not caused by
memory pressure) are being reported with
`containerStatuses[*].state.terminated.reason = "OOMKilled"` and
`exitCode = 143` (SIGTERM), even when there is no evidence of memory
pressure at the time of termination.

This was originally reported against kOps
(kubernetes/kops#18040), but the classification logic that sets this
field lives in kubelet/the container runtime rather than the cluster
provisioning tool, so filing here with sig-node's attention.

/sig node

### What did you expect to happen?

For non-OOM terminations such as node drains, liveness-probe-induced
restarts, or manual pod deletions, we'd expect:
- `container.state.terminated.reason` to NOT be `OOMKilled` when the
  exit code is 143 (SIGTERM implies graceful termination, not a
  kernel OOM kill which uses SIGKILL/137), or
- the pod-level `status.reason` to indicate `Evicted` / node shutdown
  while the container termination reason stays consistent with the
  actual signal received.

This misclassification breaks downstream tooling (alerting,
observability platforms) that rely on
containerStatuses[*].state.terminated.reason to distinguish real OOM
events from expected evictions/restarts.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a cluster on Kubernetes v1.32.x (kube-proxy v1.32.10)
2. Run a workload pod with resources.requests.memory: 512Mi and no
   memory limit set
3. Let the pod run for an extended period
4. Trigger a node drain not caused by memory pressure, e.g.:
   kubectl drain <node> --force --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
   (also reproduced via ASG scale-in / node termination handler and
   via rolling updates that cordon & drain)
5. Observe kubectl get pod <ns>/<pod> -o yaml after termination

### Anything else we need to know?

- container_memory_working_set_bytes for the affected container was
  stable around ~350-370 MiB before termination, well below the
  512Mi request
- container_oom_events_total for the container was 0 at and after
  termination
- Kubernetes events for the pod showed reason=Unhealthy (liveness
  probe failure), with no OOM-related events
- Reproduced multiple times across different pods/nodes

  confirm additional environment details (node OS, cgroup version)
